For this hope presupposes of course that man in his inner
being is dissatisfied with all that the world can offer of beauty
and nobility, with all its values and all its demands; it pre-
supposes that man suffers because of the actual condition of
the world, when he sees that life and death are here inter-
locked in an unending struggle, that evil always holds the
greater sway over man's heart, and that man despairs of ever
being able to establish on this earth a kingdom of righteous-
ness and love.
Do we belong to those who suffer in the world as it is?
Have we this hope glowing in our hearts? To-day we hear
voices loudly raised and in no uncertain manner, to declare
that such a hope is not only a childish dream but is actually
pernicious and morbid, since it incapacitates people to
perform the work that is required to be done; and that for
these reasons it should be fought and conquered by all
possible means. And in this struggle which is now engaged,
it is being said: what is the origin of such a hope? It origin-
ates with Israel and the Jews! with Jewish prophets and
dreamers! All that is essentially foreign to our own way of life.
We must not allow ourselves to be led astray by such
voices even if the picture they draw were true. But it is not
true. Suffering in face of this present world is familiar not
only to the Old Testament, but to all peoples everywhere.
And the hope of a time of deliverance, in which sorrow and
pain will be banished from the earth by divine aid, is by no
means confined to Israel but is widespread throughout the
world. It is with justice that the Christmas hymn declares:
"With longing hearts have the nations waited for Thee,
until the time was ripe!"
All over the earth there has always been the living hope
in a return of paradise, a restoration of the early golden age,
when there was no pain and no wrong on earth. The north
Germanic tribes as well as the Aryan Persians regarded the
world as the sphere of a struggle between two forces, those
